extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent attorneys, judges, and law students handling U.S. patent equity cases
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing what defenses and procedural devices may be pleaded, pleaded by plea, raised by motion to dismiss, or require answers in United States equity patent litigation; also when supplemental/revivor bills and hearings are appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seventh defence—construction of claims not proper in plea
rubrics_metrics.description: The seventh defence involves construction of the claims of the letters patent and therefore is not proper matter for a plea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letters patent are not void merely because they describe something not shown in the original application; only when they claim something not indicated or described in the specification or drawings of the original application are they obnoxious to this defence. The question what letters patent claim is a question of law for the court and cannot properly be raised by plea, demurrer, or motion to dismiss because the court must construe the claims and compare them with the original application, which must be introduced as evidence. This defence therefore should be set up in the answer (except where the complainant takes the initiative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eighth defence—statutorily required to be in the answer
rubrics_metrics.description: The eighth defence is not proper matter for a plea because statute requires it to be set up in an answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short statutory directive: certain defences must be pleaded in the answer; they cannot be raised by plea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ninth/Tenth defences—joint or sole invention as pleads only with personal knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Either the ninth or the tenth defence (based respectively on joint or sole invention) may be treated as pleas where the defendant actually knows the fact of joint or sole invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each of these defences rests upon a single matter of fact which, if decided against the complainant, is fatal to the patent. Historically it was unwise to plead them because of replication/foreclosure issues, but they may be pleaded if the defendant genuinely knows the facts alleged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eleventh defence—must state factual details in answer
rubrics_metrics.description: The eleventh defence belongs with other defences (third, fifth, sixth, and eighth) that must be set up in the answer and the answer must state the details of the facts upon which the defence is based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These defences are of a character that requires factual detail in the answer rather than bare pleas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twelfth defence—insufficiency of specification not suitable for plea or motion
rubrics_metrics.description: The twelfth defence (that the specification is not full, clear, concise, and exact enough to enable making and using the invention) cannot be made by motion to dismiss nor by plea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A defendant might be able to swear that he, a person skilled in the art, cannot make/use the invention from the specification, but cannot oath that the same is true of all skilled persons. Thus such a defence requires evidentiary proof and belongs in the answer/record rather than in a plea; it is inappropriate for a motion to dismiss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thirteenth defence—construction-of-claims issue; motion or answer but not plea
rubrics_metrics.description: The thirteenth defence depends on construction of the patent claims and not on matters of fact that can be sworn to by plea, so it cannot be treated as a plea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It can be made by motion to dismiss where profert of the letters patent has been made or they are otherwise part of the bill; an answer is also a proper pleading to interpose this defence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourteenth defence—depends on necessity for disclaimer; set up in answer
rubrics_metrics.description: The fourteenth defence was generally required to be set up in an answer because it primarily depends upon the necessity for a disclaimer and that necessity depends upon the claim being obnoxious to one or more of the first three defences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the interplay among defences (especially those not suitable for pleas) determines need for disclaimer, the answer is the proper vehicle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fifteenth defence—not proper subject for plea; depends on original patent validity/operativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: The fifteenth defence is not proper subject-matter of a plea because it depends upon the original patent being inoperative or invalid due to defective/insufficient specification, or upon lack of novelty in part of the original patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It may depend on construction of the original patent or proof that persons skilled in the art could make/use the invention from the original specification; statements of legal construction or universal factual claims are not suitable in a plea. It cannot be raised by motion to dismiss unless the original letters patent are incorporated in the bill and the question is solely one of construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sixteenth defence—reissue comparison and delay; motion if originals proffered
rubrics_metrics.description: The sixteenth defence depends partly on comparative construction of the original and reissue patents and partly upon proof that delay in applying for reissue was unreasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where both original and reissue are proffered/incorporated in the bill the defence may be made by motion to dismiss because the court can make the comparative construction and must be satisfied the delay is excused in the bill. Where the original patent is omitted, the defence must be treated as ordinary matter for an answer because it involves mixed questions of law and fact unsuitable to a plea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seventeenth defence—comparative construction requires answer or motion, not plea
rubrics_metrics.description: The seventeenth defence depends on comparative construction of original and reissue patents and may be made on motion to dismiss where both documents are proffered; otherwise it must be made in the answer and is never proper matter for a plea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the issue is one of construction (law) rather than a swearing-of-facts appropriate to a plea, it belongs in motion or answer practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eighteenth defence—double patent identity; motion if identity plain
rubrics_metrics.description: The eighteenth defence (alleging that the later patent is a double of a prior patent) may be made by motion to dismiss where the bill is based on the prior patent as well as on its alleged double.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A plea is unsuitable unless the disputed claim(s) in the subsequent patent can be plainly seen to be identical with claim(s) in the prior patent; if construction is required to determine identity the matter is one of law and improper for plea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nineteenth defence—plea ok with personal knowledge of record
rubrics_metrics.description: The nineteenth defence is suitable for a plea if the defendant has personal knowledge of the record he pleads and thus is able to make the required oath that such a record exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal knowledge enabling the oath is the key requirement for treating this defence as a plea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twentieth defence—expiration (including foreign patents) rarely a plea or motion unless on face of bill
rubrics_metrics.description: The twentieth defence (patent expired when the alleged infringement occurred) can be made by motion to dismiss where the bill shows the patent had expired at the relevant time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is seldom so because expiration relied upon is nearly always due to expiration of some foreign patent for the same invention, not apparent on the face of the U.S. patent. Where the defence depends upon a foreign patent not mentioned in the bill it cannot be taken by motion to dismiss, nor is it proper matter for a plea, since it involves comparative construction of patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twenty-first defence—unmarked sale/notice; plea possible and effect on remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: The twenty-first defence (that complainant made or sold specimens during the life of the patent without marking them 'patented' and the defendant was not duly notified or, if notified, immediately discontinued) is proper subject-matter for a plea if defendant knows the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defence need not be pleaded because the complainant must negative it in his bill/evidence; however it is waived unless presented to the court at hearing and cannot be first raised on appeal. It is not a defence to a prayer for an injunction but is a defence to a prayer for damages and to profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twenty-second defence—title defects may be motion to dismiss when on face of bill
rubrics_metrics.description: The twenty-second defence may be made by motion to dismiss where the bill sets forth copies of the complainant's title papers (or pleads them according to legal effect) so that title appears defective on the face of the bill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: where defendant knows a paper in the chain was executed after assignor had assigned to another and the prior assignment was recorded within three months, or where assignor assigned later for value more than three months after making the assignment set up in the bill and without notice to junior assignee—such facts defeat the action. No defect due to an outstanding unrecorded document can be availed without being pleaded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twenty-third defence—license must be specifically pleaded as a plea
rubrics_metrics.description: The twenty-third defence (license) is properly the subject-matter for a plea if the defendant is sure of the fact of the license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When stated as a plea it must state the character of the license specifically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twenty-fourth defence—release treated like license re pleading timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The twenty-fourth defence (release) should be treated in pleading like the twenty-third (license), and this applies whether the release was executed before or after filing of the bill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleading should specify character and timing of the release as necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twenty-fifth defence—non-infringement: motion to dismiss only if obvious from bill
rubrics_metrics.description: The twenty-fifth defence (non-infringement) may be interposed by a motion to dismiss where the bill sets forth the claims alleged to be infringed and the particular character of the defendant's doings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such motions will be dismissed except where non-infringement is obvious from the bill without reference to prior art. If motion denied, defendant may plead non-infringement in answer and support with evidence within five days after denial. U.S. precedents generally do not permit pleas of non-infringement though English equity practice might. Economical drafting can sometimes make non-infringement apparent on the face of the bill but that is usually difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twenty-sixth defence—estoppel/res judicata may be pleaded; former records usable without special pleading
rubrics_metrics.description: The twenty-sixth defence (estoppel/res judicata) may be made as in a plea and ought to be so when defendant is certain he can prove facts amounting to an estoppel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the defence consists of res judicata, the former record can be introduced in evidence without being specially pleaded in the answer; former records of actions at law may be examined to determine facts found by jury. If bill asks for damages and profits, a prior action at law may bar recovery for periods subsequent to the prior action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twenty-seventh defence—statute of limitations may be motion to dismiss when time clear on bill
rubrics_metrics.description: The twenty-seventh defence (statute of limitations) may be interposed by motion to dismiss where the bill clearly states when the infringement occurred or the period during which it was carried on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutes of limitation have same effect in federal equity as in law; if bill merely alleges infringement during life of patent and part of that life is time-barred, the applicable statute must be set up to avail defendant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twenty-eighth defence—defect may be raised by motion or answer depending on whether defect is apparent
rubrics_metrics.description: The twenty-eighth defence may be interposed by motion to dismiss or by answer in accordance as the defect appears on the face of the bill or extrinsically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the defect appears in the bill the motion is appropriate; otherwise the answer is the vehicle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolition of general and special replications—answer puts case at issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to the Equity Rules of 1913 a general replication was required; both general and special replications have been abolished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless the answer asserts a set-off or counterclaim, no reply is required without special court order; the cause is deemed at issue upon filing of the answer and any new or affirmative matter in the answer is deemed denied by the plaintiff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of subordinate bills required before decree (four kinds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four kinds of subordinate bills sometimes required before decrees for infringement can be entered: (1) Supplemental bills; (2) Bills in the nature of supplemental bills; (3) Bills of revivor; (4) Bills in the nature of bills of revivor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these as distinct procedural devices with specific uses and prerequisites described in following sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental bill—when required and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A supplemental bill is required where original bill was filed by executor/administrator or assignee in bankruptcy/insolvency when another person succeeds to title; also necessary to subject estate of defendant who becomes bankrupt; proper against stranger who conspires or purchases infringing business pending suit; proper where patent extended after filing and defendant continues to infringe; and where a new patent covering some feature of defendant's doings arises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A supplemental bill merely alleging defendant modified structure but still infringes is demurrable; some courts permit proof of new acts under original bill, others require independent suit; supplemental bill not allowed solely to bring in officers of corporate defendant after accounting. Leave of court is prerequisite to filing supplemental bills; leave obtained upon proper cause and due notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bill in the nature of supplemental bill—assignment of rights after filing
rubrics_metrics.description: A bill in the nature of a supplemental bill is called for where the original bill was filed by a person in his own right and that right passes to another by voluntary assignment or passes to assignee in bankruptcy/insolvency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule applies where entire right or part/right of one of several complainants passes. Such a bill may be maintained even if filed after expiration of the patent provided the original bill was filed before expiration and could have been maintained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bill of revivor—reviving abated suit after death
rubrics_metrics.description: A bill of revivor is the proper means of reviving and continuing an action in equity for infringement which has abated by death of one or more parties; it is to be brought by or against the executor or administrator, not heirs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant may be required to file an answer denying that the filer is entitled; state statutes of limitations may apply to bills of revivor in diverse ways (limitation counting may start at death, suggestion of death, or service of scire facias); time bars vary by state (roughly six to eighteen months). If filed in time by proper person the action stands revived without new pleadings; if defendant died without sufficient answer the bill of revivor should pray that the person be compelled to answer the original bill and its amendments. Prior testimony remains usable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bill in the nature of revivor—assignment then death
rubrics_metrics.description: A bill in the nature of a bill of revivor is required where the complainant in the original bill assigned the right and the patent and then died before the assignee took his place by a bill in the nature of a supplemental bill would have done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bills of revivor proper only by privies in law (executors/administrators); bills in the nature of revivor are available to privies in estate (assignees, devisees) to draw to themselves benefits of original action; applicable where executor/administrator prosecuting action dies and other representative steps needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bill of revivor and supplement—combination allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: A bill of revivor and supplement is a compound bill combining supplemental and revivor aspects and is proper when facts justifying either are present in the same action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any two or more of the four subordinate bill types may be united when their justifying facts co-occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave of court required for supplemental and revivor bills
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave of court is a prerequisite to filing supplemental bills or bills in the nature of supplemental bills, and likewise for bills of revivor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leave must be obtained upon proper cause shown and due notice to the opposite party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleadings to revivor bills and supplemental bills—when required
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleadings may or may not be required to a bill of revivor or a bill in the nature of a bill of revivor, but defendants are always required to plead to supplemental bills and bills in the nature of supplemental bills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the bill shows on its face that the filer was not a proper person to do so, the objection may be made by motion to dismiss; formerly such objections could be pleaded as a plea, but under modern equity rules they are set for special hearing or motion practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of hearing—judge(s), judge and jury, or master
rubrics_metrics.description: A hearing of an action in equity for patent infringement may take place before one judge sitting alone, several judges sitting together, a judge and a jury, or before a master in chancery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges are the best tribunals for patent cases, but other methods may be used at the court's discretion. Interlocutory hearings (after evidence on validity/infringement taken but before account) and final hearings (after master's account) have different focuses; preliminary hearings for injunctions treated elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlocutory hearing significance and discontinuance rule
rubrics_metrics.description: An interlocutory hearing occurs after evidence relevant to validity and infringement has been taken and before referral to master; the interlocutory hearing is generally pivotal; a complainant cannot discontinue his action when called for hearing without showing better reason than an intention to begin a new suit hoping for a stronger case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If interlocutory hearing results in dismissal it becomes final. Courts will examine all patentability and construction questions involved and will not refrain from doing so at suggestion of either party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources and rules for questions of law in patent equity cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions of law in equity patent cases are to be decided according to relevant rules of law and equity in force in United States courts, derived from U.S. statutes and decisions of U.S. federal courts and certain pre-Constitution English chancery decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Later English decisions are persuasive but not binding; state court decisions analogous. Where U.S. statutes direct following particular state laws, those state laws are binding on federal judges. Decisions strictly relevant and well-reasoned may be followed even if from English or state courts, but differing statutory contexts or fallacious reasoning justify disregard.
